products.title: DIY CO2 Generator Kit — 2 L Stainless
products.body_html:
A refill-free CO2 kit for planted tanks. Citric acid and bicarbonate react inside a 2 L stainless bottle to produce CO2 — no gas cylinder, no trips to a refill shop.

  • No cylinder to refill. You top it up with two cheap dry chemicals instead of hauling a bottle to a gas supplier. That is the whole point of this design.
  • Constant-pressure valve body tested above 50 kg/cm² with a 3 kg regulated output and an automatic release above 30 kg.
  • Kit includes the 2 L stainless bottle, pressure gauge and valve, diffuser, 2 m of CO2 tubing, four suction cups, a 300 ml measuring cup, a funnel and two sets of reagent.

What this is not: a pressurised cylinder system. It is a chemical generator. Output tapers as the reaction exhausts and needs recharging every few weeks depending on your bubble rate. If you want set-and-forget pressurised CO2, buy a regulator and a refillable cylinder instead — this is the cheaper, more hands-on route.

  • Max and min memory. A spot reading tells you nothing about the overnight swing. This holds both extremes until you reset it.
  • Probe in the water, display outside. No hunting for an angle to read a glass thermometer through a planted foreground.
  • 0.1 °C resolution, °C or °F. Fine enough to see the difference between a stable tank and a heater cycling too wide.
  • Suction cup and adhesive pad. Mount the display on the cabinet or the glass, and route the probe behind the hardscape.

faqs.a: Usually because they are in different places. Water stratifies, especially in a tank with low flow. Put both in the same spot for a fair comparison.

faqs.q: Can I calibrate it?
faqs.a: No, it is a fixed ±1 °C sensor. For stability tracking that is plenty; if you need certified accuracy you want a lab probe.

products.title: Glass Lily Pipe Set — Inflow & Outflow
products.body_html:
A matched pair of borosilicate glass pipes that replace the black plastic intake and spraybar most filters ship with. The outflow returns water in a rolling surface curve; the slotted inflow draws evenly without pinning fish against it.

  • The reason aquascapers switch. Glass disappears against the background. Plastic intakes are the single most visible piece of hardware in an otherwise clean tank.
  • Surface agitation without a ripple tank. The outflow curve breaks the surface film and helps gas exchange, which matters more once you are injecting CO2.
  • Slotted intake. Wide slots pass debris to the filter instead of clogging, and keep shrimp and fry out of the impeller.
  • Borosilicate, not soda-lime. Thicker walls and better thermal tolerance. Still glass — see the FAQ on cleaning.
